Se o vilão da história tenta construir uma mensagem criando uma mitologia própria, enquanto absorve símbolos conhecidos para conferir veracidade à sua construção, com o reforço do choque visual ou até conceitual dos ocorridos, o filme em si é a tentativa de Fincher em fazer o mesmo. Ambos sentem a necessidade de cobrir tudo o que pensaram, explicando cada detalhe para quem recebe a mensagem, e esquecem que o vácuo, o desconhecido, também importa para uma mitologia. O incompreensível pode ser um conceito muito favorável para um filme e para o espectador, pois força ambos a irem além do que está posto, a pensar de verdade. Os personagens e as divisões internas na blocagem da montagem do filme podem parecer, à primeira vista, uma estrutura organizacional interessante, mas a antecipação e o ritmo são muito mal trabalhados, nunca alcançando algo harmonioso em tela. A imagem capturada é tão desinteressante que até mesmo o choque visual - que poderia ser um truque para prender a atenção - contribui para o afastamento do espectador em relação a um filme que nada diz com essas imagens difíceis de serem assistidas.

Había dejado de usar Letterboxd porque estoy viendo demasiadas cosas y muchas del festival y de la facultad, pero por favor: esta película, ya me acordé por qué siempre me pareció una porquería. Un par de cuestiones, escritas al tuntún: 1. La lógica de los pecados se va al carajo. Durante toda la película te explican que Doe mata gente porque encarna un pecado y hasta él mismo se justifica enumerando a sus víctimas en la escena del auto. De repente (y antes de ese discurso, según la diégesis) nos enteramos de que mató a Tracy, que es inocente, porque siente envidia de Mills. ¿Para qué me explicaste toda la lógica anterior? Si al final no importa en lo absoluto. Además no tiene sentido, hermano; la película te quiere vender que realmente hay una lógica detrás, ¿pero de qué tiene envidia de Mills si ni lo conoce? ¿Por qué justificar todos tus asesinatos si ya rompiste esa lógica? Se pisa los talones a sí misma. Pésimamente construida. 2) Mills no tiene ninguna oportunidad de salvar a Tracy. No es una tragedia causada por un error suyo: Doe ya la mató antes de que él supiera lo que estaba pasando. Lo único que puede hacer es dispararle o no dispararle, una supuesta decisión moral ridícula. No hay suspenso ni posibilidad de fracaso, porque el guion simplemente lo pone en una situación en la que Mills desde el vamos no tiene ninguna responsabilidad. Es una película cruel con sus personajes. 3) Doe es un pelotudo que la película te quiere pintar de genio. Deja pistas completamente arbitrarias para que Mills y Sommerset lleguen exactamente donde él quiere: lo de pintar los ojos de la foto, el cuadro dado vuelta, la palabra y la frase de Milton atrás de la heladera, etc. Al principio comprás que el tipo lo tiene todo calculado, pero cuando pensás dos segundos te das cuenta de que muchas cosas funcionan solamente porque el guion decide que Sommerset va a interpretar exactamente lo que Doe esperaba. Eso y todo lo construido alrededor de John Doe no tiene ni pies ni cabeza, pero me guardo lo más importante para la próxima: 4) Lo de la biblioteca. Es directamente ridículo y encima es la única razón por la cual lo encuentran. Hay tres libros que todo católico culto (y más uno obsesionado con la teología) tiene: la Biblia, la Suma Teológica y la Divina Comedia. El tipo es un fanático de los pecados capitales que supuestamente lleva años estudiando teología y tiene un conocimiento supuestamente erudito sobre el tema, pero resulta que la pista fundamental son los libros de Santo Tomás, Dante, Chaucer y compañía (además de sumar al cocktail libros protestantes como el Paradise Lost, excelente poema que recomiendo muchísimo) que alquiló en una biblioteca. ¿Cómo no va a tener sus propias ediciones? Es ilógico. Y además, ¿Nadie más estudia teología? ¿El genio asesino y conocedor de teología no podía comprarse una Suma Teológica? — Soy un fanático católico conocedor de teología y voy a empezar a matar porque hay pecadores en el mundo moderno. — ¿Tenés la Suma Teológica? — No, la saqué de la biblioteca. — ¿Y la Divina Comedia? — También. — ¿Y la Biblia? — Esa también la devuelvo el martes. Dejate de joder… 5) Los personajes están mal construidos a otro nivel. La película confunde crueldad con profundidad. Tracy prácticamente existe para que la maten y el embarazo parece agregado para que la escena sea todavía más cruel. Y Mills ya era un tipo iracundo desde el principio, así que tampoco hay una verdadera caída en eso. Podría haber matado a Mills y después a sí mismo por envidioso (¿¿envidia de qué??). Encima termina con la frase de Hemingway como si acabáramos de leer a Dostoievski, es realmente una guasada. Entretiene, eso sin duda. Pero es a costa de que a la propia película no le importe nada de lo que está sucediendo: verdaderamente no le importa ni la teología, ni los personajes, ni la trama; todo para un golpe de efecto al final.

A little disappointment for me. I am not a huge fan of classic police thrillers, even though I have watched many of them, and Se7en is in line with stereotypical American thrillers. Indeed, it’s about two investigators conducting an investigation into a crazy serial killer, except there is nothing original here; it’s too bland. Moreover, all the cases are foreseeable and expected, as the killer openly shows the detectives that his victims represent a specific deadly sin. It seems as if David Fincher wanted his thriller to be a global success, as he adds all the easy elements for his film to be broadly appreciated. Moreover, Brad Pitt doesn’t play that well here, according to me. The setup and the first act are also way too long. How many scenes of small talk do we have to undergo before the plot starts to get exciting ? Nevertheless, the turning point, although late, is good. The final confrontation is also decent but not that shocking or surprising for the spectator. I can’t help comparing Se7en with Prisoners . I think that Prisoners is a textbook example of what a thriller should be: it’s refined, visually soothing, and the plot is just perfect. On the contrary, Se7en is weak. To conclude, the “seven deadly sins” that John Doe follows aren’t from the Bible, as many could think. The concept traces back to Evagrius Ponticus, a Christian monk living in the Egyptian desert in the late 4th century. He wasn’t trying to build a moral code for everyone, he was writing practical guidance for monks trying to master their own minds during long stretches of solitude and temptation. He identified eight “evil thoughts” that troubled the ascetic life (he added “sadness,” which was removed later). Dante's Purgatory cemented the seven deadly sins in Western moral imagination. In the poem, Mount Purgatory is shaped like a mountain with seven terraces, one for each sin, stacked in order of severity (worst to least severe). Souls climb the mountain, working through one terrace at a time, purging themselves of that particular sin before moving up to the next. The order is : Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Greed, Gluttony, Lust.

Tengo opiniones bastante encontradas con Se7en porque realmente me gustó muchísimo el desarrollo de la película, la investigación, las pistas y la forma en la que vamos conociendo a John Doe, me parecía que la película estaba construyendo algo con muchísimas posibilidades narrativas y durante gran parte de ella sentía que cada detalle tenía una razón para estar ahí. Doe claramente quería que alguien lo encontrara y que alguien pudiera observar su obra, incluso cuando Somerset y Mills llegan a su departamento se siente que Doe está impresionado por haber sido encontrado y que realmente existía una construcción alrededor de la investigación que me parecía excelente. El problema para mí aparece principalmente en el final y no porque no entienda lo que la película quiere hacer, de hecho entiendo perfectamente la intención de que Mills termine representando la ira y que Doe construya las condiciones necesarias para que Mills termine matándolo. El problema es que siento que la película justifica el final pero no lo desarrolla de la mejor manera posible. Para mí existe una diferencia muy importante entre que un acontecimiento pueda ser justificado dentro de la historia y que realmente haya sido construido narrativamente para que ese acontecimiento sea una consecuencia natural de todo lo anterior. El caso de Tracy es el ejemplo más importante. El plan de John Doe comenzó antes de que Mills fuera asignado como compañero de Somerset, por lo que Mills aparece dentro de la historia de una manera bastante circunstancial y posteriormente Doe adapta su obra alrededor de él. Contextualmente se puede justificar que Doe envidia la vida de Mills, que ve en él aquello que él mismo no tiene y que por eso decide convertirlo en la representación de la ira, pero narrativamente siento que la película no construyó suficientemente la relación de Mills con Tracy para que su muerte tuviera el peso que necesitaba tener. Tracy termina siendo fundamental para el final pero durante gran parte de la película no existe un desarrollo suficiente de ella como para sentir que estamos llegando inevitablemente a esa tragedia. Por eso también me parece extraño cuando Doe habla de su “obra maestra” como si todo lo que ocurrió hubiera estado construido específicamente alrededor de Mills, cuando realmente la película nos muestra un plan que existía antes de que Mills estuviera involucrado. La explicación existe, pero siento que aparece principalmente para poder justificar el desenlace que la película ya necesita. Para mí una revelación puede ser algo que jamás vi venir, pero cuando finalmente aparece debería poder mirar hacia atrás y pensar que todo estaba ahí, que las acciones anteriores de los personajes y las circunstancias de la historia produjeron naturalmente ese resultado. En Se7en yo no tuve completamente esa sensación, tuve más la sensación de que entiendo por qué Doe decidió hacerlo pero no siento que la película haya construido suficientemente las condiciones para que tuviera que hacerlo de esa manera. También me sucede algo parecido con Somerset durante la escena final. Somerset entiende perfectamente lo que está ocurriendo, intenta convencer a Mills de que no mate a Doe porque sabe que hacerlo significa que Doe gana, pero la forma en la que responde durante la escena me parece extraña respecto a su propia motivación. Si realmente quiere impedir que Mills lo mate, esperaba una reacción mucho más desesperada y física, intentando acercarse a él, detenerlo o ponerse entre ambos, porque Mills tiene varios segundos para tomar una decisión mientras Somerset simplemente intenta convencerlo. No digo que solamente exista una manera realista de reaccionar, pero dentro de lo que la película había construido de Somerset, su comportamiento me pareció demasiado conveniente para que Mills pudiera llegar exactamente al resultado que la historia necesitaba. Y esto es lo que más me decepciona porque la tesis de la película me parece excelente. El problema no es el nihilismo, ni que el final sea oscuro, ni siquiera que Doe consiga ganar. El problema es que siento que la tesis está mucho mejor construida conceptualmente que dramáticamente. La película sabe perfectamente qué quiere decir con Mills convirtiéndose en ira, pero siento que tuvo que acomodar algunas decisiones de los personajes para poder llegar a esa conclusión. Para mí la profundidad narrativa está mucho más relacionada con la relación entre la motivación de un personaje y las acciones que produce esa motivación. Un personaje tiene determinados valores, deseos, miedos y circunstancias, y a partir de eso debería tomar decisiones que produzcan el desarrollo de la historia. Cuando ocurre así, el final no solamente se justifica, sino que se siente como una consecuencia de todo lo que vimos. En Se7en siento que en algunos momentos ocurre lo contrario, que el final necesita que determinados personajes hagan determinadas cosas y posteriormente la película encuentra una explicación para que esas cosas tengan sentido. Me hubiera gustado muchísimo más que la película desarrollara a Mills como el protagonista central, que conociéramos mucho más su vida, su relación con Tracy, su personalidad y sobre todo su obsesión con demostrar que puede ser un buen detective. Que la investigación de Doe fuera progresivamente convirtiéndose en una obsesión personal y profesional, que Mills comenzara sacrificando aspectos de su vida por resolver el caso y que finalmente esa obsesión terminara produciendo la pérdida de Tracy y su transformación en ira. De esa manera la muerte de Tracy no sería solamente el elemento necesario para completar los siete pecados, sino la consecuencia de una relación que nosotros ya conocemos y que hemos visto desarrollarse durante toda la película. Incluso siento que Somerset podría no haber sido necesario como protagonista secundario si la película hubiera profundizado mucho más en Mills. Su presencia funciona muy bien para contrastar dos formas de entender el mundo y la investigación, pero al mismo tiempo divide el protagonismo y hace que Mills no tenga todo el desarrollo psicológico que para mí necesitaba tener para que el final realmente me destruyera. Se7en es una película que me parece muy buena durante gran parte de su desarrollo y cuya idea final me parece incluso excelente, pero para mí existe una diferencia entre tener una conclusión interesante y construir perfectamente el camino hacia ella. El final se puede explicar, se puede justificar y tiene una tesis muy clara, pero siento que la película no consiguió desarrollar todas las condiciones necesarias para que yo sintiera que ese final era una consecuencia inevitable de los personajes y no solamente la conclusión que la historia necesitaba alcanzar. Me hubiera gustado ver una película donde la profesión, la obsesión, la familia, el sacrificio y finalmente la pérdida de Mills fueran construyendo poco a poco su transformación en ira. Creo que con ese desarrollo Se7en podría haber sido una de mis películas favoritas, porque la investigación de John Doe y la tesis que plantea tienen muchísimo potencial, pero para mí la construcción narrativa del final se siente demasiado impuesta y eso termina quitándole profundidad a una película que conceptualmente tenía muchísimo más para desarrollar. To say the least, I was a little bit disappointed after having heard really good reviews about the movie. I was going into this movie expecting to watch a deeply psychological murder mystery like what it portrays itself to be. Although, after finishing the movie I don’t think they really quite hit the mark with that. My main issue with the movie is the fact that it seems like things just happen. For instance, though Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman are both detectives/investigators, I felt as though they did very little detective work to figure things out. Majority of the movie is them showing up to the crime scenes of each “sin” (after other personnel have already investigated) and then it’s Morgan Freeman stating the obvious fact that the killer is using the pattern of the seven deadly sins. All of the “detective work” that is done just seems predictable and superficial just to progress the story. Another example of this is the fact that Pitt and Freeman don’t even actually catch the antagonist; he voluntarily turns himself in. Granted, they were on his trail at a point, I just think it’s lazy writing to have him turn himself in, especially after just running from them a few days ago. Even still, the best part of this movie was by far the main antagonist who is only really present for the final 3rd act of the movie. I think Kevin Spacey does a really good job portraying an emotionless, psychotic serial killer though he lacks a proper script. I really enjoyed the dynamic and tension between Spacey and Pitt, but I just couldn’t help but question why? I’m not sure if I just missed that part of the movie, but why did Spacey choose Pitt. What was his motive? Not only that, but, not to sound heartless, are we as the audience supposed to care about the final twist in the end with the package? It didn’t really feel like they built much on Pitts personal life outside of work, so why would we care about Pitts’ significant other? I don’t know I think overall the movie just felt a little undercooked.

Se7en is a film which attempts to wear many hats. On one hand you have attempts at a highly interesting and flashy serial murder case which operates as the major stopping points of the story. Each of the murders is extreme and profane, crafted with this kind of blunt detail that’s certainly entertaining, but ultimately surface level and less well thought out than they likely intended. On the other you have an extremely standard buddy cop framework between the two main characters which makes no real attempt at straying away from convention. Both of these central building blocks are joined together by this phenomenal, nearly noir, presentation which sets up the film as something which is both easily entertaining and contains more for those who are willing to seek it out. Unfortunately, I found Se7en ultimately ends up confused in this crossroad of seriousness and entertainment, ultimately ending up lingering at the surface level and only utilizing these bigger ideas as window dressing rather than something which builds towards something greater. Unfortunately the signs are there from the beginning. The characters in this film are prototypical to a degree which ends up being serviceable but lacking both in terms of story progression and intrapersonal drama. Brad Pitt plays a standard hotshot new detective, willing to prove himself and reeking in overconfidence by his supposed credentials. Rather than demonstrating his actual abilities, Pitt prefers to crack one liners and sneer at his partner’s persistence to do his job properly rather than quickly give up the moment he faces the first sign of abstraction. Likewise, his partner, Morgan Freeman, is his polar opposite. An old blood detective who just wants to retire out of the force because of the toxic apathy of society which has eroded his sense of goodwill. He’s ultimately pragmatic about his job and knows that their efforts are more likely than not to be pointless in the grand scheme of things. This is about as standard of a setup as you can get, but the film never really causes it to head in any sort of meaningful direction. Pitt and Freeman very rarely actually interact for the first quarter of the film, and due to the extremely short timeframe of the plot, their inevitable destination as uncommon allies mere days later is unnatural and unconvincing. The two of them lack chemistry, and their lack of substantial interaction makes the buddy cop presentation lose traction as a whole. Pitt’s more than willing to speak his mind, and the film is more than willing to utilize him as the main source of entertainment, but because Freeman isn’t willing to ever give him an inch these moments end up falling flatter than they had to. This is representative of how the film handles the crux of their characters as well. Pitt and Freeman represent opposite ends of the same coin. Being detectives and thoroughly entrenched in the toxicity of low society, Pitt’s optimism and Freeman’s pragmatism could represent some kind of clash of ideals. But instead, Se7en chooses to merely float these ideas rather than tackle them directly. This is most blatantly presented in a scene in a bar about halfway through the film. Freeman is telling Pitt about how he’s fed up with all of the apathy of society, how people are so willing to take the easy way out rather than work through their problems, which ultimately is the source of their misfortune. Society does not care about itself and so Freeman does not care about society. Pitt rejects this idea, not for any actual stated reason or counterargument, but merely because he cannot accept this line of thought. He states that Freeman himself is also taking the easy way out, which is true, but does little to shift his perspective in any meaningful way. This idea remains a loose thread rather than being properly explored, and this trend can be observed with much of the rest of what Se7en aims to accomplish. The other core principle of Se7en is, of course, the murders. This aspect is where the film really shines. Se7en is already a visually impressive film, perfectly capturing the kind of grime which makes up this low society by operating primarily with low blues and greys. This is a very dark film, but the main attribute I would give the visual quality is dirty. The murders primarily take place in these low income locations, even the apartment buildings are worn down and damaged. Despite the primary weather condition being rain this ends up reminding me of mud more so than dirt being washed away. This translates to the murders perfectly. Each of which are immensely brutal and highly creative, making use of the sin motif more as a suggestion for a gory creative artpiece than anything. My favorite ended up being the first of the murders, representing gluttony you have this obese man who was forced to eat himself to death, but not before cutting off an entire pound worth of meat off his body. This is far and away the most visually stimulating of any of the murders, and perfectly builds up the case as something which is equal parts sadistic and incredible. While grotesque, the visual quality makes it more entertaining than disgusting, and the absurdity of the murders themselves adds to this feeling. Of course, the problem lies with how these murders are presented. For the first half of the film, the duo is convinced that the murders are inspired by famous literary works such as The Divine Comedy and The Canterbury Tales due to them representing the titular seven sins. The film spends a significant amount of time showcasing them researching and discussing these ideas leading you to believe that these would be significant details to the case. Unfortunately, this ends up being nothing more than a wild goose chase, and these details are nothing more than window dressing than any kind of greater idea. Once you reach the halfway point, the film is more than willing to abandon this idea and pivot back towards the cops stumbling in the right direction rather than solving the murders from their own ideas. Of course, the books do end up being brought up again as a key plot point, but it’s only done so to a superficial degree rather than being an integral aspect of how the murders are conducted. This wouldn’t be so much of a problem had the film not spent as much time as it did during the set up period showcasing these works and explaining how they relate to the case. It makes their investigation seem even more like a wild goose chase rather than an intellectual process, a feeling which is only amplified as the film progresses as they never manage to make it off the back foot. Much like the murders, the person who’s leading them along is equally disappointing. John Doe’s reveal in the finale of the film is nothing short of abrupt, and what he actually manages to accomplish once he reveals himself is middling at best. While the ultimate climax, the psychological destruction of Pitt’s character, is certainly very entertaining (and brought forth one of the most iconic lines in modern cinema) John leaves a lot to be desired in terms of actually being a villain. He comes across as a caricature of Hannibal Lecture but without the raw intimidation or presence. He speaks in this very monotone and vague way as a way of demonstrating his control over the situation, only truly losing his temper when he begins to speak about his victims and their respective sins. Unfortunately, he offers little additional support to the foundation of the murders, only confirming that they were executed for superficial means rather than any kind of actual greater purpose or meaning. It’s easy to see that, yes, the people he murdered are representations of the seven sins in some way, but they aren’t carried out as a result of any sort of conviction or greater purpose, but rather just as a means of “higher punishment” administered through his own means. Pitt rightfully calls him out on this, but due to the shallow nature of his character he’s unable to capitalize on this point, mirroring his lack of ability to counter Freeman. My issues with Se7en are not due to a lack of entertainment. The movie excels when it comes to simply fun, the basic nature of its core elements, which are elevated due to the higher quality of its premise, is enough to make sitting through the film worthwhile. However, the film insists that it includes higher ideas in an attempt to nudge itself into something more without properly committing. Each of its greater elements: the character’s opposite personalities, the higher purpose of the murders/how the murders are actually solved are merely thrown out and left unresolved for the viewer to take at face value rather than leaving much room for thought. The ideas being unresolved isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but they end up feeling cheap because of how little foundation they’re given, rather than the lack of a concrete conclusion. Se7en seems to present itself as a movie which is more than your standard buddy cop serial murder mystery film, but while it’s certainly higher quality than your run of the mill flick it just can’t seem to escape its simplistic roots. In the end, it chose entertainment over truly committing to what it wants to say, it takes the easy way out, though I can’t blame them for it.

A movie that spends seven days reminding us that humans are f**ked up, and somehow still manages to feel a little empty !! This is definitely well-made or the most artistic film of Fincher’s direction, the gloomy cinematography, the production design and that constant feeling of rain-soaked misery all work perfectly together. Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman are great, and the film knows exactly how to create an uncomfortable atmosphere without constantly throwing cheap jumpscares at you. The philosophy behind the film is interesting too, especially its idea of how deeply corruption, violence and human nature are connected, but I don't think it explores those ideas as deeply as it could have. The problem is the screenplay. The concept is brilliant, but the actual mystery and investigation never felt as gripping to me as it should have. A lot of the film feels like it is building toward that famous ending rather than giving us an equally engaging journey to get there. I also predicted the ending, or at least where it was more or less heading, which made it much less impactful for me. And yes, the ending is disturbing and memorable, but one great final act can't completely save a film that feels unnecessarily slow and repetitive in the middle.

Pretty enjoyable for the first three quarters, though I'm a fairly easy guy to please. Some scenes were drawn out, Brad Pitt's performance was disappointing, but the case was engaging and the kills were pretty gnarly, love to see it. The ending was pretty disappointing, right from the moment the van rolls in. I have no problem with the idea of John Doe setting up his final kills in this meeting, nor any problem at all with Doe himself being one of his targets, but I can't help but feel he would've been far better suited as the representation of wrath over envy. That "I've always admired you" shit was such an ass pull. I don't even mean in the script itself, he'd said it plenty of times before in the movie, even though I think setting up a twist like this by just repeating a line a few times is kinda lame. No, this is an ass pull in the context of Doe's character. As far as we can tell, Doe's admiration of the two detectives came from when they found his apartment. Cool. You're telling me that Doe's master plan, years in the making, ended with him deciding he fit the bill for envy because he was impressed by a couple detectives a few days before? It just seems a little impulsive for this criminal genius. I understand that John Doe is crazy, of course he is, he's a serial killer. But I can't help but feel that he would've been a far more interesting character if he saw himself as the embodiment of wrath. If he was more self aware about his work, and more aware of his role in it as the wrath of what he sees as the divine, I think the ending would've been way stronger than him fucking over Brad Pitt over some nonsense about envy. I guess it was a solid film overall, I'm just very disappointed with the ending.

Eu gosto da ambiguidade que o fincher já trouxe em outros filmes dele que eu consegui identificar, mas acho que esse é o mais explicado que já vi dele. O que não é ruim, mas senti que faltou mais conteúdo nessa explicação. É muito fácil entender a temática degradação moral/social, não só porque o filme comunica isso por si só (fotografia, niilismo dos personagens - diálogos sobre apatia social etc), mas precisa vir alguém mais de uma vez pra explicar como aquele mundo é corrompido o suficiente pra permitir o mal retornar a ficar solto. Ao mesmo tempo que me pega muito o lance de que nem todos os assassinatos são mostrados com frieza suficiente como outros, sendo que claramente cada morte poderia tocar em mais pontos mais profundos, mas são descartados ou por falta de desenvolvimento, ou uma aceleração proposital da montagem. Mas além do que eu já mencionei, esse corte ainda é muito coeso como apenas investigação, já que a relação dos personagens funciona muito bem por todo o filme, e os minutos finais são realmente de grande impacto. Mas honestamente não entendo filmes como Clube da luta , Garota exemplar e outros como silêncio dos inocentes , No country for old men , serem considerados bastante abaixo desse filme, ou não tão clássicos quanto, apesar de serem filmes posteriores a esse de 95. Foi uma grande fonte de inspiração deles, tenho certeza. Como eu disse, como investigação, é um ótimo thriller. Merece aclamação. Enfim. Um ótimo filme.
